title: Justin Jefferson Has Become UNDERRATED, And Will Bounce Back
text: This is Justin Jefferson's comeback season and it's not just about a quarterback change for him.  Let me explain. You're listening to Locked On Vikings, the daily Minnesota Vikings podcast, part of the Locked On Podcast Network.  Your team every day. How is everyone?  Welcome to the Locked On Vikings podcast where we're always trying to learn something new.  Today's episode is brought to you by FanDuel.  Get a guaranteed $350 bonus bet when you bet $5 every day for 7 days. Follow all the action at fanduel.com. Today is City Hall Tuesday.  That means I'll be answering your questions sent to me via Google Doc in the show notes. So, if you have any questions or bold predictions for the end of the week , you can embed them in the Google Doc link found in the show notes for every episode of Locked On Vikings. Today's first question comes from Avi.  He asked, "In Matt Harmon's mapping for Justin Jefferson, he discussed how Jefferson is now not being used around the formation as much as in 2022 or 23. And the fact that he's mostly positioned outside makes him double-guarded at a rate no other wide receiver has seen in the last 10+ years of wide receiver season mapping. Do you have a compelling reason why the KOC isn't putting JJ in the slot or off the line of scrimmage as much as they used to?"  This is an interesting question.  I love this question.  I'll start with something a little simpler and come back to it later.  Because I believe this is the year of awakening. So, here's the thing.  Justin Jefferson statistically had the worst season of his career last year.  It's not just because of the surrounding factors, right?  When we say maybe we get a little bit of an improvement at the quarterback position and that will work.  Of course that would be part of his argument. But there were also times last year where Jefferson didn't play as well as he has in the other four seasons of his career .  There are times when he's awake, he gets a little less separation than we're used to seeing from him.  He missed a couple of catches, he had a weird game against the Ravens.  I mean, there are moments like that, right?  So, if we want to get up, we say, "Hey, it was just a fluke." "It won't happen again."  And I think that's a pretty easy argument to make.  Um, but this issue of outside versus in-slot placement is an interesting angle.  Matt Harmon, his reception perception mapping is highly respected.  So, we quote the right person.  So, there are a few thoughts that immediately come to mind regarding the main question. Why do we put them more often outside and less in the slots?  The answer has to do with who else is in that attacking line. Hockenson, Addison, deal with whoever the other wide receiver is .  In the past, Jalen Nailor was the one who often played the slot position. And the other thing is, if they want to make those reads, progressive reads like left to right or right to left, the outermost player will be the primary read.  So, you have to choose, do we put Jefferson outside or make him the last read in the progression? And they chose to put him early in the progression to try to get him the ball more often, right?  That also makes perfect sense.  So, that's one thing that could happen, but another thing is sharing the field with Addison. So, the key to the question, right?  Kevin O'Connell put Jefferson in the slot , in bunch formations, and two- man stacks much more often in '22 and '23, then lessened that in recent years, I think because of Jordan Addison.  Jordan Addison needs that freedom of movement and most games won't be able to provide that freedom for two different people.  One gets freedom of movement, whether they are the moving player or they are in a specific position in the stack or bunch, but one has to deal with the pressure.  Someone has to face it and someone doesn't have to face the pressure.  Well, Jefferson had a lot of different tools to beat the pressure.  I would say the press man is probably the best strategy against him, but that doesn't mean it's a surefire way to counter him.  Jefferson has a way to defeat him. Addison has fewer ways.  He had to break his route a little, go further out of his way to do it, and he always did.  He's very good at using his speed, getting back up, re-routing, but it would have been a little more impactful.  So, it makes sense to me to give Jordan Addison some freedom of movement and tell Justin Jefferson, " go out there and win some duels ."  We know you can do it .  So, that might be one of the reasons.  Part of the reason could be trying to create an offensive structure that fits that quarterback, right?  '22 and '23, well, those were the Kirk Cousins ​​years.  Sam Darnold might want to get better at, you know, reading that area of ​​the field, and they might try to do the same with J.J.  McCarthy too.  How they do with Kyler Murray , that remains to be seen.  So, that could change and this could be one of those little positioning details that Kevin O'Connell tinkers with when there's a different quarterback. Everyone wants to be like Kevin .  asked, "You've discussed the concept of choice routes in the past and how receivers have the ability to change these routes to get around defenders. Similarly, quarterbacks must identify their positions to be able to throw with anticipation and timing. When playing against a defense like Flores' that rotates coverage after the snap, how do these routes work when you don't know where the opponent is, or are these concepts simply not worth running against this defensive scheme ?"  So, the Vikings often see the choice route of other Shanahan-McVay teams like the Packers.  There will be a version of their choice.  So, it's really effective against coverage rotation.  You will see camouflage and rotation all the time.  And the answer to your question is that this is not a pre-snap reading.  Pre-snap information is helpful, isn't it?  If you see someone running a choice and there's a linebacker in the box and you're going to run play action with another one or there's some other reason to believe that there's motion that you think will make that guy shift or something like that.  You'll think, "Okay, he's never going to get to an outside leverage position. This option is either going to be spot or it's going to open outside. I know that now."  And as a quarterback, you can take that little shortcut if you can figure out what the opposing defense looks like.  However, in the end, the linebacker may not be the one guarding this area.  He might actually be being guarded by a cornerback due to a complicated coverage rotation or a safety moving forward or something.  So, this is absolutely a read that should happen in the first few moves of the game and once you reach the top of your drop, the coverage is already clearly visible.  There's no more disguise once you get there. Coverage is coverage.  At that point, if you still try to bluff with a cover three pattern but show cover two, you are actually already in cover two position because your opponent will throw the ball and you will still be in cover two position. So, therein lies the problem, this is not a pre-snap read.  The information before the snap is helpful, but it 's the reading after the snap, where you can no longer hide your intentions.  And after that it's just a matter of feeling the pressure of the opponent, right?  If he is on my inside, I will direct the ball away from the defender. Or, if there are no defenders nearby, I'll aim the ball straight at him.  The receiver of the ball should feel the same way, but the decision should be based on spatial awareness and very, very fast processing.
